speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you are experiencing double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and upper limb weakness. To understand the cause of these symptoms, could you tell me when these issues first started and if they worsen with exercise or improve with rest?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: Those symptoms strongly suggest a neuromuscular issue. Do you experience any difficulty swallowing or speaking, and have you noticed any drooping of your eyelids? REQUEST TEST: Creatine_Phosphokinase (CK).

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the confirmation; normal CPK levels help rule out primary myopathies. Given your worsening weakness with activity and specific eye movement issues, could you clarify if you have a family history of muscle disorders or if you have been diagnosed with diabetes or thyroid disease? REQUEST TEST: Antibodies for Myasthenia Gravis (Anti-AChR, Anti-MuSK) and Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, Free T4).

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Acetylcholine_Receptor_Antibodies: Present (elevated); Thyroid_Function_Tests: TSH - Normal, Free_T4 - Normal.

speaker: Doctor
text: The positive Acetylcholine Receptor Antibodies confirm an autoimmune etiology, strongly supporting a diagnosis of Myasthenia Gravis. Given the diplopia on gaze and limb weakness that fatigues, do you have a history of thymoma or do you currently experience shortness of breath? REQUEST IMAGES: Chest_X-Ray.

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis. The combination of fatigable diplopia, proximal limb weakness, elevated anti-AChR antibodies, and normal thyroid function confirms this autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder. The negative Chest X-Ray helps rule out an associated thymoma.
